findings.title: No Content-Security-Policy header anywhere in the stack
findings.principle: Every response served by solen.ch carries a Content-Security-Policy header. Ship it first in Report-Only mode for one full deploy cycle with an explicit allowlist (self plus js.stripe.com, maps.googleapis.com, the Mapbox GL host, PostHog's ingest host, Google's font/avatar hosts already allowlisted in next.config.mjs images.remotePatterns), verify the violation report log is empty for that cycle, then flip to enforcing Content-Security-Policy. No inline <script> without a nonce or hash once enforced.
findings.why: React auto-escapes JSX, but 7 files in this codebase call dangerouslySetInnerHTML (confirmed by security.md's own grep, salon layout + 4 category pages + SalonDetailV3.tsx) for JSON-LD structured data, and at least some of that data plausibly includes a salon's own free-text bio field, which is attacker-adjacent content flowing through an escape hatch. With zero CSP, a single missed-escaping bug in any of those 7 call sites has no second line of defense: the injected script simply runs. CSP is the standard backstop precisely for this class of bug (OWASP CSP Cheat Sheet), and Solen has never had it.
findings.local_evidence: netlify.toml lines 22-36: two [[headers]] blocks list X-Content-Type-Options, X-Frame-Options, Referrer-Policy, X-DNS-Prefetch-Control, Permissions-Policy, Strict-Transport-Security, Cache-Control -- Content-Security-Policy is absent from both. next.config.mjs's headers() function (lines 106-115) sets only Referrer-Policy. middleware.ts's only header-setting code (grepped) is the CORS Access-Control-Allow-* pair, no CSP. Three independent places that could set it; none do.
findings.absence_proof: grep -n 'Content-Security-Policy' netlify.toml next.config.mjs -> 0 hits. grep -n 'Content-Security-Policy\|CSP' middleware.ts -> 0 hits. find . -iname '_headers' -not -path '*/node_modules/*' -> no file (so no alternate Netlify header mechanism exists either). Cross-checked against _backend-system/research/security.md section 6, which independently reaches the same conclusion via the same three files.
findings.existing_coverage: Full: _backend-system/research/security.md section 6 already researched this exhaustively (Netlify sends zero headers by default, the exact rollout method, the nonce-vs-allowlist tradeoff) and names it the single highest-value gap in the whole security file. The research is complete; only the LAW.md freeze and the actual header never happened. This finding restates it here because it is squarely in this domain's scope (security headers) and remains unfixed as of this session.
findings.where_it_should_live: _backend-system/LAW.md (does not exist yet) plus the concrete implementation in netlify.toml's [[headers]] block for '/*'.
findings.enforcement: gate: a CI or pre-deploy check that greps netlify.toml for a Content-Security-Policy line and fails the build if absent, mirroring the existing white-only-web-gate.py pattern already used elsewhere in this codebase for a different frozen rule.

findings.title: No CI gate for dependency vulnerabilities, and no Dependabot/Renovate; a live critical CVE sits in the lockfile undetected between manual audits
findings.principle: Every push to main and every pull request runs `npm audit --omit=dev` (or an equivalent SCA scanner) as a CI job that fails the build on any new critical or high finding versus a checked-in baseline count, the same ratchet pattern already used for tsc and lint in .github/workflows/quality.yml. Additionally, Dependabot (or Renovate) is configured for automatic weekly dependency-update PRs so a fix that ships upstream reaches Solen within days, not only when someone happens to re-run npm audit by hand.
findings.why: A vulnerability scan is only as good as the last time someone remembered to run it. Solen's own research file (security.md section 13) already found this exact state (1 critical, 2 high, 17 moderate) on 2026-07-16; running the identical command myself on 2026-07-26 finds 1 critical, 5 high, 18 moderate, 24 total, i.e. the high count nearly tripled in ten days with zero automated signal anywhere in that window. CI enforces typecheck and lint on every push already; dependency vulnerabilities are equally machine-checkable and currently get none of that enforcement.
findings.local_evidence: npm audit --omit=dev --json run live this session: {'info': 0, 'low': 0, 'moderate': 18, 'high': 5, 'critical': 1, 'total': 24}. The critical is protobufjs (transitive via posthog-js's OpenTelemetry exporter), the highs include next itself (pinned at 15.3.8, below every relevant fix floor per security.md section 13) plus lodash (transitive via recharts) and others. .github/workflows/quality.yml contains typecheck/lint/test/e2e/visual jobs (read in full) with zero npm-audit or SCA step anywhere.
findings.absence_proof: grep -n 'audit\|CVE\|vulnerab' .github/workflows/quality.yml -> 0 hits. find . -iname 'dependabot*' -not -path '*/node_modules/*' -> no file. ls .github/workflows/ -> cron-jobs.yml, db-migrate.yml, invariants.yml, inventory-freshness.yml, quality.yml, none of which run npm audit (confirmed by reading quality.yml in full and grepping the other four for 'audit').
findings.existing_coverage: partial: security.md section 13 documents the finding and recommends upgrading next, but frames it as a one-time fix ('upgrade next to the latest 15.x patch') rather than naming the missing recurring GATE that would have caught the high-count regression between the two audit runs. No doc anywhere proposes wiring npm audit into CI.
findings.where_it_should_live: _backend-system/LAW.md plus .github/workflows/quality.yml (a new job) and a new .github/dependabot.yml.
findings.enforcement: gate: a new CI job in quality.yml, ratchet-style like the existing lint job (baseline = current count, fail if it goes up), plus dependabot.yml for automatic PRs.

findings.title: No general mechanism for tracking credentials with a known future expiry; the concrete Apple case lives only in prose
findings.principle: Every credential that has a known or foreseeable expiry (a signed-JWT OAuth client secret, a time-boxed API key, a cert Solen itself manages rather than Netlify's auto-renewed TLS) is recorded in one machine-readable place (e.g. a CREDENTIAL_EXPIRY.md table with columns: credential, expiry date, re-mint command, and owner) with a scheduled reminder (a GitHub Actions cron or a scheduled-tasks entry) that fires at 30 days and 7 days before expiry. A credential's expiry date is never allowed to live solely in a chat memory file or a paragraph of prose documentation with no automated trigger.
findings.why: Apple's OAuth client-secret JWT for Solen's Sign in with Apple integration expires 2026-12-30 (per project memory project_money_features_shipped.md and _docs/BACKEND.md line 98, both citing the same date). If that date passes unnoticed, every customer using Sign in with Apple is locked out with no code-level warning beforehand; Apple auth would simply start failing in production. Today the only artifact tracking this is a memory file and a doc sentence, both of which require a human to remember to check them; there is no cron, no dashboard, no CI check, nothing that would surface the deadline on its own the way a build failure or a lint error would.
findings.local_evidence: project memory /Users/sulo/.claude/projects/-Users-sulo-Documents-solen/memory/project_money_features_shipped.md: 'Secret JWT EXPIRES 2026-12-30: re-run node scripts/mint-apple-secret.mjs <p8> 54C4J53STX ch.solen.web TCW6MHM3UW + re-paste in Supabase Auth > Providers > Apple.' _docs/BACKEND.md line 98 repeats the same date and explicitly notes 'this is pure ops/config, not code in this repo, there is nothing to grep for it here.' scripts/mint-apple-secret.mjs exists in the repo but nothing calls it on a schedule.

CronList / scheduled-tasks tooling was not queryable from this read-only research agent, but grep of .github/workflows/*.yml for 'apple' or 'mint-apple-secret' returns 0 hits, confirming no CI/cron references the script either.
findings.existing_coverage: none for the general mechanism. The Apple-specific instance is documented (in prose, twice) but that is documentation of the fact, not a system that enforces or reminds.
findings.where_it_should_live: A new CREDENTIAL_EXPIRY.md at repo root or in _backend-system/, plus a GitHub Actions scheduled workflow (cron: monthly) that diffs today's date against the table and opens an issue or emails ADMIN_EMAIL when a row is within 30 days.
findings.enforcement: gate: the scheduled workflow itself is the enforcement (fails/notifies on approaching expiry); a lighter first step is a checklist entry, but a genuinely durable fix needs the cron, not just a doc, given this exact class of failure (a memory-only deadline) is what nearly bit Solen once already per the memory file's own framing.

findings.title: No documented or enforced rotation cadence for routine (non-leaked) secrets
findings.principle: Every server-held secret (Stripe live/test keys, STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET, SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY, RESEND_API_KEY, CRON_SECRET, BOOKING_HMAC_SECRET, LOYALTY_HMAC_SECRET) has a written rotation cadence in one place, even a simple one: rotate on any team-member offboarding or access-scope change, and rotate the Stripe/Supabase/Resend keys at least annually regardless. Absent a specific reason to rotate sooner, this is the floor, not a suggestion; a secret with no rotation date is a secret nobody has ever rotated.
findings.why: A secret's usefulness to an attacker who obtains it (via a leaked log, a compromised laptop, a departing team member's local .env.local copy) never expires unless the secret itself is rotated. OWASP's Secrets Management Cheat Sheet names rotation as a primary control precisely because the alternative (no rotation) means a secret leaked at any point in the product's history remains valid forever until someone happens to change it for an unrelated reason.
findings.local_evidence: lib/env.ts's serverEnvSchema (read in full) validates 15+ server secrets by format (sk_/whsec_/re_ prefixes, min-length checks) but has zero rotation metadata; .env.example lists the same secrets with no rotation note. No file anywhere states a cadence.
findings.absence_proof: grep -rni 'rotat' across _backend-system, _docs, _rules, CLAUDE.md, .github -> only two hits, both about DATA retention (backup-recovery.md discussing backup rotation, not secret rotation) and the webhooks.md research file's own forward-looking section 14 (outbound secret rotation for a system that does not exist yet). Zero hits for any INBOUND/live-secret rotation cadence.
findings.existing_coverage: partial: _backend-system/research/security.md section 10 already names this exact gap explicitly ('no documented rotation cadence for any secret') and recommends the same fix (a simple written cadence). The research is done; the doc was never written and nothing was frozen into LAW.md.
findings.where_it_should_live: _backend-system/LAW.md, a short new section, or a SECRETS.md at repo root.
findings.enforcement: checklist (a rotation cadence is an operational habit, not something CI can verify actually happened); the closest machine check is the credential-expiry cron from finding 03 extended to cover 'last rotated' dates, not just hard-expiry dates.

findings.title: No leak-response runbook: what to do in the first hour after a secret is confirmed exposed
findings.principle: A one-page runbook exists naming, per secret class (Stripe secret key, Stripe webhook secret, Supabase service role key, Resend key, CRON_SECRET, HMAC secrets): (1) where to revoke/regenerate it (which dashboard, which button), (2) what breaks immediately upon rotation and in what order to redeploy so the break window is minimized, (3) who/what needs to be told (a salon-facing integration does not exist yet, so today this is purely internal, but the runbook should say that explicitly rather than assume it), (4) whether a dual-secret transition window is possible for that specific secret (Stripe already supports this for the webhook secret specifically) or whether rotation is a hard cutover with a guaranteed short outage.
findings.why: This project's own security research names its founding security incident as 'exposed credentials in git' (security.md section 10, citing _rules/SECURITY_RULES.md). A leak-response runbook is the concrete artifact that turns 'we know this happened once' into 'we know exactly what to do the next time it happens', and today that knowledge does not exist anywhere except as an implicit assumption that whoever is on duty will figure it out under pressure, which is precisely the condition under which mistakes compound (rotating the wrong key, missing a downstream consumer that still has the old key cached, forgetting the CRON_SECRET is shared across every /api/cron/* route so ALL of them break simultaneously on rotation with no built-in grace period).
findings.local_evidence: app/api/cron/no-show/route.ts:17 and every other /api/cron/* route reads a single CRON_SECRET with no fallback/grace period (a plain !== compare against one value), so rotating it is a hard, simultaneous cutover across every scheduled job with zero built-in transition window, unlike Stripe's own webhook-secret rotation which explicitly supports dual-secret verification. This asymmetry (one secret rotates gracefully, most others do not) is exactly the kind of detail a runbook would surface before an incident, not during one.
findings.absence_proof: grep -rni 'incident response\|runbook' across _backend-system, _docs, _rules, CLAUDE.md -> 0 hits. grep -rni 'leak.*secret\|secret.*leak' across the same paths -> 0 hits outside the webhooks.md research file's own forward-looking outbound-rotation section (which is about a future salon-integrator-facing secret, not Solen's own inbound secrets).
findings.existing_coverage: none. webhooks.md section 14 covers the OUTBOUND (salon-facing) rotation case in depth but explicitly for a system that does not exist yet; it does not cover Solen's own existing inbound secrets (Stripe, Supabase, Resend, CRON_SECRET) leaking, which is the more urgent, live-today case.
findings.where_it_should_live: A new RUNBOOK.md or a section in _backend-system/LAW.md.
findings.enforcement: doc-only (a runbook is read at incident time, not enforced by a gate); the closest machine-checkable piece is confirming the CRON_SECRET-has-no-grace-period design decision is deliberate and documented, not accidental.

findings.title: No secret-scanning gate in CI or pre-commit, despite the project's own founding incident being exactly that failure mode
findings.principle: Every push and pull request runs a secret-scanning tool (gitleaks or detect-secrets, either as a GitHub Action or a pre-commit hook) that fails the build on any string matching a known secret-format pattern (sk_live_, whsec_, re_, a Supabase JWT shape, an AWS-style key, etc.) newly introduced in the diff. GitHub's own push protection (if the repo is on a plan that includes it) should also be confirmed enabled as a second, platform-level layer, not relied on as the only layer since it does not catch every custom secret shape (e.g. Solen's own HMAC secrets have no recognizable prefix pattern GitHub would know to flag).
findings.why: '.gitignore ignores .env files' is a preventive control that only works until someone bypasses it (git add -f, a secret pasted into a comment, a secret hardcoded temporarily 'just for testing' and forgotten). A scanning gate is the detective control that catches the case the preventive control missed, which is exactly the scenario the project's own documented founding incident describes.
findings.local_evidence: _rules/SECURITY_RULES.md line 7 (cited by security.md section 10) names 'exposed credentials in git' as the incident that triggered the current S1 security rule stack. .gitignore lines 31-34 and 95-96 (read directly) correctly ignore .env/.env.local/.env.*.local/.env.production/.env*.bak*, which is the preventive half already done correctly; there is nothing on the detective half.
findings.absence_proof: find . -iname '*.pre-commit*' -not -path '*/node_modules/*' -> no file. grep -rn 'gitleaks\|detect-secrets\|trufflehog\|git-secrets' across the whole repo including .github/workflows -> 0 hits. security.md section 10's own Unverified list explicitly names this exact open question ('Whether GitHub secret-scanning / push protection is actually enabled on the Solen repo... not visible from the local working tree'), i.e. even the research pass could not confirm the platform-level backstop is on, and no repo-level scanning fills that gap regardless.
findings.existing_coverage: partial: security.md section 10 recommends this exact fix ('confirm GitHub secret scanning / push protection is enabled... a settings check, not a build') but frames it as a one-time settings check, not a standing CI gate; a settings toggle a GitHub admin could silently turn off later has no re-verification mechanism, whereas a checked-in CI step does.
findings.where_it_should_live: A new .github/workflows/secret-scan.yml plus _backend-system/LAW.md noting the requirement.
findings.enforcement: gate: the CI workflow itself (gitleaks-action or equivalent, fails the build on a match).

findings.title: Stripe integration uses one full-access secret key everywhere; no least-privilege Restricted Keys
findings.principle: Server contexts that only need a narrow slice of the Stripe API (e.g. a future read-only reporting job, or any new integration that doesn't need to create charges or manage payouts) use a Stripe Restricted Key (rk_live_/rk_test_) scoped to exactly the resources/actions that context needs, rather than the platform's single full-access sk_live_ key. The full secret key is reserved for the code paths that genuinely need broad access (the webhook handler, which reacts to any event type, and the payment-intent/Connect-transfer creation paths).
findings.why: A single full-access key used across every Stripe-touching route (charges, transfers, disputes, payouts, Connect account management, webhook verification) means any code-injection or SSRF-adjacent bug in ANY one of those routes has the blast radius of the ENTIRE Stripe account, not just the specific capability that route actually needs. Stripe's own Restricted Keys feature exists specifically to shrink that blast radius; least-privilege API keys is also explicitly named in this domain's scope brief.
findings.local_evidence: lib/env.ts's STRIPE_SECRET_KEY schema (read in full) only validates the sk_live_/sk_test_ prefix, never rk_live_/rk_test_. The webhooks.md audit file confirms the Connect/refund/dispute/payout logic all lives in the one route.ts file, and the same key is used across that file plus create-payment-intent, booking-pay-intent, walkin/pay-intent, and every other Stripe-touching route (all read the same STRIPE_SECRET_KEY via getServerEnv()).
findings.absence_proof: grep -rn 'rk_live\|rk_test\|restricted key' --include='*.ts' --include='*.md' across the whole repo (excluding node_modules) -> 0 hits anywhere, confirming no Restricted Key is used or even discussed.
findings.existing_coverage: none. Neither webhooks.md nor security.md mentions Stripe key scoping at all; both files' 'least privilege' discussion is scoped to RLS/DB access, not third-party API key scope.
findings.where_it_should_live: _backend-system/LAW.md, a new subsection under secrets, plus lib/env.ts's format-validation comment once implemented.
findings.enforcement: checklist for now (this requires provisioning work in the Stripe dashboard, not something a static grep can enforce until multiple key types actually exist in the schema); once implemented, a gate could check that a given route imports the correctly-scoped key.

findings.title: Outbound-webhook design law (HMAC scheme, retry, ordering, SSRF, rotation) is fully researched but never frozen, for a system that will eventually exist
findings.principle: Before any future session builds Solen's first outbound webhook sender (a salon POS/calendar integration, a partner notification feed), the design decisions already researched in webhooks.md sections 8-14 (Standard Webhooks HMAC-SHA256 over id.timestamp.payload, 5-minute default tolerance, Svix's 8-attempt exponential-plus-full-jitter retry schedule, best-effort ordering with a sequence field, DNS-rebinding-resistant SSRF re-checking at send time, dual-secret rotation windows) are copied into a frozen LAW.md, not re-derived or substituted with a training-memory guess by whichever session happens to build it.
findings.why: This is precisely the failure mode this whole audit exists to catch: deep, correct research already exists (14 fully-sourced sections, a decision-candidates table, named tradeoffs) but sits in a research/ file that a future session has no obligation to read before writing code, versus a LAW.md that IS the canonical, must-read-first source per this project's own stated layer model. A future session under time pressure building 'a quick webhook sender' is exactly the scenario where a weaker, invented-from-memory HMAC scheme gets shipped instead of the researched Standard Webhooks convention, silently regressing months of research work.
findings.local_evidence: webhooks.md's own intro (lines 3-5) states explicitly: 'A repo-wide grep... found zero outbound webhook system in the codebase today; sections 8-14 are therefore forward-looking design law for a system that does not exist yet.' The orchestrator's own brief confirms _backend-system/LAW.md, RATIONALE.md, AUDIT_2026-07-16.md and QUESTIONS.md do not exist on disk despite README.md promising them.

findings.existing_coverage: full research, zero frozen law. This is the domain's clearest instance of the 'research exists but no frozen law' shape the orchestrator specifically asked to be surfaced.
findings.where_it_should_live: _backend-system/LAW.md (to be created), a dedicated Outbound Webhooks section copying the section-8-14 recommendations verbatim.
findings.enforcement: doc-only until a system exists to gate; once an outbound sender is built, a code-review checklist item referencing the frozen LAW.md section is the practical enforcement.

findings.title: The live Stripe webhook has no default: case, so a newly-enabled event type silently no-ops forever with zero log signal
findings.principle: Every switch/if-chain that dispatches on an external system's event type ends with an explicit catch-all branch that logs the unhandled type (a plain console.warn or a lightweight audit row is sufficient) before returning success, so a forgotten case for a newly-enabled event type is discoverable in logs rather than permanently invisible. This is required specifically because a silent no-op that also returns 200 leaves no trace anywhere that it happened.
findings.why: Solen's project CLAUDE.md already names 'a control/column/filter that LOOKS wired but does nothing' as this codebase's number one silent-failure mode; an unhandled webhook event type is the exact same failure shape applied to event-type coverage instead of a DB filter. The webhook file's own header comment (route.ts:17-20) lists only 7 event types while the switch implements 12, meaning the comment itself is already known-stale, which is a small but concrete sign this class of drift already happens in this exact file.
findings.local_evidence: app/api/stripe/webhook/route.ts:69-900 (per the existing audit file's own file:line citation) has no default: case in its switch(event.type); an unmatched type falls through to the bare `return NextResponse.json({received:true})` at line 911 with zero log line.
findings.absence_proof: This is a verified, already-cited code gap (not something I re-derived): _backend-system/audit/webhooks.md's own per-principle table marks WEBHOOK-06 as GAP with the identical file:line citation, and the research file's decision-candidates table independently recommends the same fix.
findings.existing_coverage: full: both the research (webhooks.md section 6) and the audit (audit/webhooks.md WEBHOOK-06 row) already name this exact gap with the exact one-line fix. This finding is included here only because the orchestrator's brief asks for what is STILL not covered after months of law-layer building, and this is a real, still-open, already-identified-twice code gap that has nonetheless not been fixed. It belongs in this report as a reminder that identification is not the same as closure.
findings.where_it_should_live: app/api/stripe/webhook/route.ts itself (a one-line code fix, not a new doc).
findings.enforcement: gate: near-impossible to generically lint 'switch has no default', but a targeted grep-based pre-commit check for this specific file would work if this file is deemed important enough; otherwise this is a one-line fix that should simply be applied.

findings.title: No enforcement gate for 'every secret comparison must be constant-time'; the rule is written in one file's comment and has already drifted
findings.principle: A repo-wide check (grep-based CI step or pre-commit hook) flags any `!==`/`===` comparison where either operand is a variable named or typed like a secret, token, or signature (a naming-convention-based heuristic: SECRET, TOKEN, SIGNATURE, HMAC in the variable or env-var name) and requires crypto.timingSafeEqual on equal-length buffers instead, with a documented exception list for any deliberate non-secret same-named variable.
findings.why: The project already has the correct RULE written down (lib/bookings/guest-access.ts's own header comment states 'compare with crypto.timingSafeEqual (NEVER !==)') and correctly follows it in five separate call sites (resend-access, walk-in-verify, quick-action, walkin/confirm, loyalty-qr). But a rule that lives in one file's comment, with no mechanical check, does not travel: every /api/cron/* route compares CRON_SECRET with a plain !== (confirmed still true this session), violating the codebase's own documented standard. CWE-208 (Observable Timing Discrepancy) is a real, named vulnerability class with at least one 2026 CVE of exactly this shape (Trilium's sync-endpoint timing attack, cited in security.md section 9); 'we wrote the rule down once' has already proven insufficient to keep it followed everywhere it applies.
findings.local_evidence: app/api/cron/no-show/route.ts:17: `if (authHeader !== \`Bearer ${cronSecret}\`)`, a plain string compare, verified live this session (unchanged since security.md's 2026-07-16 finding). grep across both /Users/sulo/.claude/hooks and the project's .claude/hooks for 'timingSafeEqual' or 'constant.time' or 'timing.safe' returns 0 hits, confirming no gate exists to catch this pattern anywhere in the two-layer hook estate.
findings.absence_proof: grep -rli 'timingSafeEqual\|constant.time\|timing.safe' /Users/sulo/.claude/hooks /Users/sulo/Documents/solen/.claude/worktrees/quirky-ellis-ef5559/.claude/hooks -> 0 hits in either hooks directory (134 + 30 hook scripts total per the domain brief, none of them check this).
findings.existing_coverage: partial: security.md section 9 already documents the CRON_SECRET violation as a named, low-severity, easy-to-fix finding, and correctly credits guest-access.ts as the pattern to copy. What is missing is any mechanism that would have caught the drift automatically instead of requiring a manual audit pass to notice it, which is the actual missing principle here (a gate, not a restated rule).
findings.where_it_should_live: .claude/hooks (project-level, alongside the other 30 project gate scripts) as a new pre-edit or pre-commit check.
findings.enforcement: gate: a new grep-pattern-based hook analogous to the existing drift-check hooks already in this codebase (e.g. pre-edit-drift-gate.sh's pattern-matching style).
